before.content_html:
Why Body Systems Matter in Sport

Every movement you make in sport — a sprint finish, a tackle, a shot at goal — depends on at least four body systems working in harmony. Sport scientists, physiotherapists and coaches all need a solid understanding of how these systems are structured before they can make sense of how the body responds to exercise. This lesson focuses on the body system structures you are required to know: the skeletal system, the muscular system, the cardiovascular system and the respiratory system.

The Skeletal System

The skeleton is the body's rigid framework. It is made up of 206 bones in an adult and is divided into two main parts: the axial skeleton (skull, vertebral column, ribcage) and the appendicular skeleton (limbs, shoulder girdle, pelvis). Bones are classified by their shape. Long bones — such as the femur, humerus, tibia and fibula — act as levers during movement. Short bones (wrist and ankle bones) provide stability and support. Flat bones — the cranium, scapula, ribs and pelvis — protect vital organs. Irregular bones include the vertebrae of the vertebral column. The main bones you must know are: the cranium (skull), clavicle, scapula, humerus, radius, ulna, ribs, vertebral column, pelvis, femur, patella (kneecap), tibia and fibula.

Key Fact

The main bones you must know are: cranium, scapula, humerus, radius, ulna, ribs, vertebral column, pelvis, femur, patella, tibia and fibula. Work from head to toe and you will not miss any.

Types of Joint and Synovial Joint Structure

Where two or more bones meet, a synovial joint allows free movement. All synovial joints share the same basic structure: a joint capsule encloses the joint, lined by the synovial membrane which secretes synovial fluid to lubricate and nourish the articular cartilage. Articular (hyaline) cartilage covers the ends of bones, reducing friction. Ligaments connect bone to bone, stabilising the joint. The three synovial joint types you need to know are: ball and socket joints (shoulder and hip — allow movement in all planes), hinge joints (knee and elbow — allow flexion and extension only) and pivot joints (top of the vertebral column/atlas and axis — allow rotation).

A synovial joint contains six key structures that work together to allow smooth, pain-free movement. The joint capsule is a tough fibrous sleeve enclosing the whole joint. Inside it, the synovial membrane produces synovial fluid — a viscous liquid that lubricates and delivers nutrients to the articular cartilage. Articular cartilage (hyaline cartilage) coats the bone surfaces, reducing friction and absorbing compressive forces during impact. Ligaments are strong bands of connective tissue that hold bone to bone, preventing dislocation. Some joints also contain bursae (fluid-filled sacs) to cushion areas of friction, and in the knee, fibrocartilage menisci deepen the joint surface and distribute load.

The Muscular System

There are three types of muscle tissue in the body. Cardiac muscle is found only in the heart and contracts involuntarily and continuously throughout life. Smooth muscle lines internal organs such as blood vessels and the digestive tract and also works involuntarily. Skeletal (voluntary) muscle is attached to bones via tendons and is under conscious control — it is the type of muscle used in all voluntary sporting movements.

The major voluntary muscles you must locate are: biceps (front of upper arm — flexes the elbow), triceps (rear of upper arm — extends the elbow), deltoids (top of the shoulder — abducts the arm), pectorals/pectoralis major (chest — adducts and rotates the arm), abdominals (abdomen — flex the trunk and stabilise the core), quadriceps (front of the thigh — extends the knee), hamstrings (rear of the thigh — flexes the knee), gastrocnemius (calf — plantarflexes the ankle), gluteals/gluteus maximus (buttocks — extends and externally rotates the hip), and latissimus dorsi (broad muscle of the back — pulls the arm downward and backward). The spec also includes trapezius (upper back and neck — elevates and retracts the scapula).

Key Fact

The major muscle groups are: biceps, triceps, deltoids, pectorals, abdominals, quadriceps, hamstrings, gastrocnemius, gluteus maximus, latissimus dorsi and trapezius. For each one, know its location on the body.

Muscle Fibre Types

Skeletal muscle fibres are not all identical. The specification distinguishes two main types. Type I (slow-twitch) fibres contract slowly, generate less force but are very resistant to fatigue. They are rich in mitochondria and myoglobin, giving them a red appearance, and they rely predominantly on aerobic respiration. They are well suited to endurance activities such as marathon running or cycling. Type II (fast-twitch) fibres contract rapidly and generate greater force but fatigue quickly. They rely more on anaerobic respiration and are recruited during high-intensity, short-duration activities such as sprinting or weightlifting.

The Cardiovascular System

The cardiovascular system consists of the heart, blood vessels and blood. The heart is a four-chambered pump located in the chest cavity, slightly left of centre. The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the body via the vena cava. From there it passes through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, which pumps it to the lungs via the pulmonary artery. Oxygenated blood returns from the lungs through the pulmonary vein into the left atrium, then passes through the mitral (bicuspid) valve into the left ventricle — the most powerful chamber — which pumps blood around the entire body through the aorta. The left ventricle has much thicker walls than the right because it must generate higher pressure for systemic circulation.

Blood travels through three types of vessel. Arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure; their thick, elastic walls absorb the surge of pressure from each heartbeat. Veins carry blood back towards the heart at low pressure; they have thinner walls and contain valves to prevent backflow. Capillaries are microscopic, single-cell-thick vessels that form networks within tissues, allowing the exchange of oxygen, carbon dioxide and nutrients between the blood and cells. Blood itself is composed of red blood cells (carry oxygen via haemoglobin), white blood cells (immune defence), platelets (clotting) and plasma (the liquid carrying nutrients and waste).

Arteries have three distinct wall layers: a tough outer adventitia, a thick middle layer of smooth muscle and elastic tissue (tunica media), and a smooth inner endothelium. This construction allows them to expand and recoil with each heartbeat (the pulse you feel at your wrist is an artery). Veins share the same three layers but their tunica media is much thinner — they operate at low pressure and rely on skeletal muscle contractions and one-way valves to return blood to the heart. Capillaries are just one cell thick (endothelium only), with no muscle or connective tissue layers. Their tiny diameter (7–10 micrometres) means red blood cells pass through in single file, maximising contact time with surrounding cells for efficient gas and nutrient exchange.

The Respiratory System

The respiratory system draws oxygen into the body and expels carbon dioxide. Air enters through the nose and mouth and passes down the larynx (voice box) into the trachea (windpipe), a rigid tube kept open by C-shaped rings of cartilage. At the base of the trachea the airway divides into the left and right bronchi (singular: bronchus), each leading into its respective lung. Inside each lung the bronchi branch repeatedly into progressively narrower bronchioles, ending in tiny air sacs called alveoli.

The alveoli are the functional units of gas exchange: their enormous combined surface area (approximately 70 m² in an adult), moist thin walls and rich capillary network allow oxygen to diffuse from air into blood and carbon dioxide to diffuse from blood into air. The two lungs sit within the ribcage; the right lung has three lobes and the left lung has two (to accommodate the heart). Breathing itself is driven by the diaphragm — a dome-shaped sheet of skeletal muscle beneath the lungs. When it contracts and flattens, it increases thoracic volume, drawing air in (inspiration). When it relaxes and rises back, thoracic volume decreases, forcing air out (expiration). The intercostal muscles between the ribs assist this process by lifting and lowering the ribcage.

The point at which two or more bones meet; in synovial joints, the joint is freely moveable and lubricated by synovial fluid.

before.content_html:
Why Functions Matter

Understanding how each body system works is the foundation of sport science. Coaches, physiotherapists and athletes all need to know what each system does — not just what it is made of — so they can explain why performance improves with training, or why it breaks down with fatigue. This lesson examines the four key systems: skeletal, muscular, cardiovascular and respiratory, and explores the specific jobs each one carries out during sport and exercise.

Functions of the Skeletal System

The skeletal system performs six important functions. First, it provides support — the vertebral column and leg bones act as a structural framework that holds the body upright against gravity, which is essential for every sporting activity from swimming to weightlifting. Second, it offers protection to vital organs: the cranium shields the brain, the ribcage guards the heart and lungs, and the vertebral column protects the spinal cord. Third, bones create movement through levers — they act as rigid levers that muscles pull on to generate movement at synovial joints. Every time a sprinter drives their leg backward or a tennis player swings their racket, a lever system is at work.

Fourth, the skeleton provides the body with its structural shape — the characteristic human silhouette is determined by bone structure, and this shape influences posture and aerodynamic efficiency in sport. Fifth, certain bones — particularly the long bones such as the femur and humerus, and flat bones such as the sternum — contain red bone marrow that carries out blood cell production. Red blood cells manufactured here carry oxygen to working muscles, making this function directly relevant to aerobic performance. Sixth, bones act as a mineral store, holding approximately 99% of the body's calcium and significant amounts of phosphorus. These minerals are released into the bloodstream when needed and are also essential for normal muscle contraction.

Key Fact

The six functions of the skeletal system are: support, protection, movement through levers, structural shape, blood-cell production in red bone marrow, and mineral storage (especially calcium and phosphorus). All six may be tested in short-answer questions.

Functions of the Muscular System

The muscular system's primary function is to produce movement through contraction. Muscles can only pull — they cannot push — so they are arranged in antagonistic pairs. At the elbow, the biceps acts as the agonist during flexion, shortening to bend the arm, while the triceps acts as the antagonist and relaxes to allow the movement. During extension — for example, a basketball chest pass — the roles reverse. The specification requires knowledge of antagonistic action at both the elbow and the knee (quadriceps and hamstrings). Muscles also have synergist muscles that assist the agonist, and fixator muscles that stabilise the joint to allow efficient movement.

Beyond movement, the muscular system maintains posture — deep postural muscles such as the abdominals, erector spinae and trapezius are in a state of continuous partial contraction to hold the body in alignment during both rest and activity. Good posture reduces injury risk and improves mechanical efficiency in sport. The muscular system also plays a major role in generating heat. Muscle contractions are only about 25% mechanically efficient — the remaining 75% of the energy released is lost as heat. This thermogenic function helps the body maintain its core temperature during exercise in cold environments, which is why vigorous activity warms you up rapidly.

Key Fact

Muscular system functions: movement via contraction (agonist/antagonist pairs), maintaining posture through continuous partial contraction, and generating heat as a by-product of muscle metabolism. At the knee, quadriceps = agonist for extension; hamstrings = agonist for flexion.

Functions of the Cardiovascular System

The cardiovascular system (the systemic or pulmonary circulatory system) has three core functions. Its primary role is the transport of oxygen and nutrients to working muscles and organs. During exercise, cardiac output increases — the heart beats faster and pumps more blood per beat (stroke volume) — so that oxygen and glucose reach the muscles rapidly enough to sustain contraction. Without this delivery, muscles would switch to anaerobic metabolism and fatigue rapidly.

The second function is the removal of waste products, including carbon dioxide and lactic acid produced during exercise. Deoxygenated blood carrying CO2 returns via the veins to the right side of the heart, from where it is pumped to the lungs (the pulmonary circuit) to release CO2 and collect fresh oxygen. Lactic acid is transported to the liver for conversion. The third function is regulation of body temperature. When the body overheats during exercise, vasodilation occurs — blood vessels near the skin surface widen, bringing warm blood to the surface where heat can be lost to the environment. When the body is cold, vasoconstriction narrows these vessels to retain core heat. This temperature-regulation mechanism is directly assessable in the written examination.

Vasodilation is the widening of blood vessels — particularly those supplying the skin — which allows more warm blood to reach the surface so that heat can radiate away from the body into the environment. This is why the skin looks flushed and red during or after vigorous exercise. Vasoconstriction is the opposite: blood vessels narrow, restricting blood flow to the skin and extremities so that warm blood is redirected to the vital organs and working muscles, conserving core temperature in cold conditions or at rest. Both processes are controlled by the autonomic nervous system and happen automatically in response to changes in core and ambient temperature. Understanding this mechanism is essential for explaining why a long-distance runner may feel warm even in cold weather.

Functions of the Respiratory System

The respiratory system drives breathing — the mechanical process of moving air in and out of the lungs. During inspiration (breathing in), the diaphragm contracts and flattens while the intercostal muscles between the ribs contract to lift the ribcage outward and upward, increasing the volume of the thoracic cavity. This reduces internal air pressure below atmospheric pressure, so air rushes into the lungs. During expiration (breathing out), the diaphragm and intercostal muscles relax, the ribcage drops inward and downward, volume decreases, pressure rises and air is forced out. At rest this happens around 12-20 times per minute; during intense exercise breathing rate can exceed 40-50 breaths per minute.

The second and most critical function is gaseous exchange at the alveoli. The alveoli are surrounded by a dense network of capillaries. Oxygen diffuses from the high concentration inside the alveoli across the thin alveolar wall into the blood (where oxygen concentration is lower), binding to haemoglobin in red blood cells. At the same time, carbon dioxide — in high concentration in the blood after being produced by working muscles — diffuses in the opposite direction, from the blood into the alveoli, and is then expelled during expiration. This process of diffusion is passive and depends on the concentration gradient being maintained: the continuous flow of blood removes oxygenated blood and brings fresh deoxygenated blood, keeping the gradient steep and exchange efficient.

The cardiovascular and respiratory systems are inseparable partners — together they form the cardiorespiratory system. The respiratory system gets oxygen into the blood and removes carbon dioxide at the alveoli; the cardiovascular system then transports that oxygenated blood to the muscles and returns deoxygenated blood back to the lungs. During exercise, both systems respond simultaneously: breathing rate and depth increase to bring more oxygen to the alveoli, while heart rate and stroke volume increase to deliver more oxygenated blood to the working muscles. If either system fails to keep up — for example, if breathing rate cannot rise quickly enough — performance drops and the athlete enters anaerobic metabolism more quickly. Exam questions often require you to link both systems when explaining why performance changes with exercise intensity.

Why Does Your Body Change During Exercise?

The moment you begin exercising, your body's systems react almost instantly to match the increased demand for energy and oxygen. These immediate responses — which reverse quickly once you stop — are called the short-term effects of exercise. Understanding them is essential for any coach or athlete who wants to explain why warm-ups, pacing and hydration matter so much in practice. The key systems affected are the cardiovascular system, the cardio-respiratory system, and the muscular-skeletal system.

Cardiovascular Changes

Your heart is a pump, and during exercise it needs to deliver far more oxygen-rich blood to your working muscles. It achieves this in three linked ways. First, your heart rate increases — the number of beats per minute rises from a typical resting rate of around 60-80 bpm to well over 150 bpm during intense activity. Second, stroke volume — the amount of blood pushed out per beat — also increases because adrenaline and returning venous blood cause the heart to contract more forcefully. Third, these two changes multiply to produce a much higher cardiac output, calculated as heart rate multiplied by stroke volume. A trained athlete can increase cardiac output from roughly 5 litres per minute at rest to over 20 litres per minute during maximal exercise.

Another important cardiovascular short-term effect is the redistribution of blood flow. At rest, blood is shared fairly evenly across all the organs. During exercise, blood vessels supplying the working muscles vasodilate (widen), while vessels to less active organs such as the digestive system vasoconstrict (narrow). This redirection ensures that the muscles receiving the hardest workload get the greatest share of oxygen and nutrients at the time they are needed most.

Key Fact

Cardiac output = Heart rate × Stroke volume. During intense exercise, both heart rate and stroke volume increase, so cardiac output rises dramatically. Blood is simultaneously redirected (vasodilation) towards working muscles and away from non-essential organs (vasoconstriction).

Cardio-Respiratory Changes

Your muscles need more oxygen and produce more carbon dioxide during exercise. The cardio-respiratory system responds by increasing both the rate and depth of breathing. Breathing frequency (breaths per minute) rises sharply — from around 12-20 breaths per minute at rest to 40-60 during hard exercise. At the same time, tidal volume — the amount of air moved in a single breath — increases because the diaphragm and intercostal muscles contract more powerfully. Together, a higher breathing rate and a greater tidal volume produce a large increase in minute ventilation (the total volume of air breathed per minute), ensuring that oxygen supply and carbon dioxide removal keep pace with the energy demands of the working muscles.

Increased body temperature is an inevitable by-product of the chemical reactions that release energy during exercise. The cardiovascular system helps manage this through vasodilation of blood vessels near the skin, allowing more heat to radiate away. Sweating is the other key cooling mechanism: sweat glands release water onto the skin surface, which evaporates and carries heat away from the body. This is why staying hydrated during exercise is so important — losing too much fluid through sweat reduces blood volume, which in turn makes it harder for the heart to maintain cardiac output.

Key Fact

Minute ventilation increases during exercise because breathing rate AND tidal volume both rise. Body temperature also increases, triggering vasodilation near the skin and sweating — the body's main mechanisms for temperature regulation during exercise.

Muscular-Skeletal Changes and Muscle Fatigue

As exercise intensity rises, the working muscles receive an increased supply of oxygen and nutrients thanks to vasodilation and the higher cardiac output described above. The muscles also become warmer, which temporarily increases their elasticity — they can stretch and contract more efficiently, reducing injury risk. However, if exercise is intense or prolonged, the muscles eventually begin to fatigue. Muscle fatigue is the inability to maintain the required force output, and athletes experience it as a burning sensation, a feeling of heaviness, and a progressive loss of power and coordination.

At high exercise intensities, when the cardio-respiratory system cannot deliver oxygen quickly enough to match demand, the muscles switch to anaerobic respiration. One waste product of this process is lactic acid. As lactic acid accumulates in the muscle tissue and bloodstream, it reduces the ability of the muscle fibres to contract effectively, contributing to the burning sensation and fatigue. The point at which lactic acid accumulates faster than the body can remove it is sometimes called the lactate threshold — going beyond this threshold rapidly accelerates fatigue. Lactic acid is eventually cleared during recovery through increased breathing and blood flow, which is one reason a gentle cool-down is important after intense exercise.

Once exercise intensity drops, the body enters a recovery phase in which oxygen consumption remains elevated — known informally as excess post-exercise oxygen consumption (EPOC). During this period, increased breathing rate and blood flow deliver extra oxygen to the muscles, which is used to convert the accumulated lactic acid back into glucose in the liver (the Cori cycle). This process is why heart rate and breathing rate stay elevated for several minutes after exercise has stopped, and why a light cool-down jog is more effective than stopping abruptly — it keeps blood flowing and speeds lactic acid removal.

At low intensities (e.g. a brisk walk), heart rate and breathing rate rise modestly, energy is supplied almost entirely aerobically, and lactic acid stays below the lactate threshold. At moderate intensities (e.g. a steady run), heart rate and tidal volume are noticeably elevated, sweating begins, and muscles start to warm up significantly. At high intensities (e.g. a 400m sprint), cardiac output is near its maximum, breathing rate and tidal volume are at peak, lactic acid accumulates rapidly, and muscle fatigue sets in quickly. The exam may ask you to compare the responses at different intensities — always link the cardiovascular, respiratory and muscular systems together in your answer for higher marks.

before.description: The permanent changes regular training produces in the cardiovascular, respiratory and musculoskeletal systems.
before.content_html:
Why Does the Body Change With Training?

When you exercise repeatedly over weeks and months, your body does more than just cope — it permanently rebuilds itself to handle the demands you place on it. These permanent structural and functional changes are called long-term adaptations. They are the physiological reason why a trained athlete performs far better than an untrained person of the same age and size. Understanding these adaptations helps coaches design effective training programmes and helps athletes appreciate why consistency is essential.

Cardiovascular Adaptations

The heart is a muscle, and like any muscle it responds to repeated overload by growing stronger. Cardiac hypertrophy is the thickening and enlargement of the heart muscle, especially the walls of the left ventricle. A hypertrophied heart pumps a greater volume of blood with each beat, so it needs to beat fewer times per minute to circulate the same amount of blood. This is why trained endurance athletes often have a resting heart rate below 60 beats per minute — a condition known as bradycardia. For an elite cyclist or marathon runner, resting heart rates of 40–50 bpm are normal.

Linked to cardiac hypertrophy is an increase in stroke volume — the volume of blood ejected by the left ventricle in a single beat. Because the ventricle has enlarged and its walls are stronger, it can fill with more blood and expel it more forcefully. Increased stroke volume means the heart achieves the same cardiac output at a lower heart rate, reducing the strain on the myocardium. Recovery after intense exercise also improves: a trained heart returns to its resting rate more rapidly because its larger stroke volume clears excess oxygen debt more efficiently. Faster recovery is therefore a direct consequence of cardiac hypertrophy and increased stroke volume working together.

Key Fact

Cardiac hypertrophy (a stronger, larger heart) leads to increased stroke volume, which in turn produces a lower resting heart rate (bradycardia) and faster recovery after exercise. These four cardiovascular adaptations are directly connected.

Respiratory Adaptations

Regular aerobic training strengthens the respiratory muscles — including the diaphragm and intercostal muscles — and increases lung capacity. Vital capacity, the maximum volume of air that can be exhaled after a maximum inhalation, increases with training. Trained athletes can move more air per breath, meaning they can deliver more oxygen to the alveoli with each respiratory cycle. The alveoli also adapt: the number and density of capillaries surrounding the alveolar walls increases through a process called capillarisation. With more capillaries in close contact with the alveoli, gas exchange — the diffusion of oxygen into the blood and carbon dioxide out — becomes faster and more efficient. The result is that a trained athlete extracts a greater proportion of oxygen from each breath.

Increased lung capacity and capillarisation work together during intense exercise: when oxygen demand spikes, the trained respiratory system can meet it more readily, delaying the onset of fatigue and allowing higher training intensities to be sustained. This improved respiratory efficiency is particularly important in endurance sports such as long-distance running, cycling and swimming, where prolonged aerobic effort places the greatest strain on the oxygen-delivery system.

Key Fact

Increased vital capacity and capillarisation of the alveoli are the two main respiratory long-term adaptations. They work together to increase the rate and efficiency of gas exchange, delivering more oxygen to the bloodstream per breath.

Musculoskeletal Adaptations

Resistance training causes muscle hypertrophy — an increase in the cross-sectional area of individual muscle fibres, particularly type II (fast-twitch) fibres. Hypertrophied muscles generate greater force, giving the athlete increased muscular strength. Endurance training increases muscular endurance by improving the muscles' mitochondrial density and glycogen storage capacity, allowing them to sustain repeated contractions for longer without fatiguing. Alongside muscle hypertrophy, capillarisation occurs within the muscles themselves: new capillary networks grow between muscle fibres, improving oxygen and nutrient delivery and accelerating the removal of carbon dioxide and waste metabolites. This muscular capillarisation is distinct from alveolar capillarisation but equally important for sustaining performance.

The skeleton and connective tissue also adapt. Repeated mechanical loading during weight-bearing exercise stimulates bone-forming cells (osteoblasts) to lay down extra mineral, resulting in increased bone density. Denser bones are stronger, more resistant to fracture, and less susceptible to stress injuries. The tendons and ligaments that support the joints also become thicker and stronger through regular training, providing better joint stability and reducing the risk of sprains and ruptures. These connective tissue adaptations are slower to develop than cardiovascular changes but are vital for long-term athletic durability.

During high-intensity anaerobic exercise, glucose is broken down without sufficient oxygen, producing lactic acid as a by-product. Lactic acid dissociates into lactate and hydrogen ions; it is the accumulation of hydrogen ions that lowers muscle pH and causes the burning sensation associated with fatigue. Regular high-intensity training triggers several adaptations that raise the point at which lactic acid begins to accumulate (the lactate threshold). Trained muscles have more mitochondria, allowing a greater proportion of energy to be produced aerobically even at higher exercise intensities, so less lactic acid is generated. The muscles also become more efficient at buffering (neutralising) hydrogen ions and at clearing lactate by converting it back to glucose in the liver. The practical result is that a trained athlete can sustain a higher workload before feeling the effects of lactic acid accumulation, directly improving performance in repeated-sprint sports and endurance events alike.

The dominant adaptations depend on the training method used. Endurance athletes (e.g. long-distance runners, cyclists) experience the greatest improvements in cardiac hypertrophy, stroke volume, bradycardia, vital capacity, alveolar capillarisation and lactic acid tolerance — all of which support sustained aerobic effort. Resistance athletes (e.g. weightlifters, rugby forwards) experience pronounced muscle hypertrophy, increased bone density and stronger tendons and ligaments, as the primary demand is generating force rather than sustaining prolonged cardiovascular output. Team-sport athletes (e.g. footballers, basketball players) gain a broad range of adaptations because their training combines aerobic conditioning with repeated high-intensity sprints and contact work. A well-designed training programme matches the training method to the desired adaptation, following the principle of specificity.

glossary_terms.definition: Permanent changes to the body's systems that result from regular exercise over weeks and months, making the body more efficient and capable.
The enlargement and strengthening of the heart's walls — particularly the left ventricle — caused by regular endurance or resistance training.
A resting heart rate below 60 beats per minute, common in trained athletes as a result of cardiac hypertrophy and increased stroke volume.
The growth of new capillary networks around the alveoli and within muscles as a result of regular training, improving the rate and efficiency of gas exchange.
